text.tspan: Slice a release · Set the goal — stage flow
a release is a GROUPING, not a time axis. the DONE condition is assembled from upstream declarations, never authored at the end.
DECISIONS are dashed · ARTIFACTS are listed right
RED — cost, or a route that leaves the stage / blocks it
GREEN — Tony's input into the work: his annotations, his corrections
BLUE — changed since you last marked this reviewed
what is already built · the framed and viability-tested candidates ·
their QUALIFIED risks with countermeasures attached · and the record
of what was already ruled out.
five factors, and lumping them together is the mistake — they act on
the grouping in three different ways.
THE CEILING IS THE UNUSUAL ONE.
almost everything sizes a release by what is READY —
a bound from the producing side. this is a bound from
the RECEIVING side: a release can be too big even when
it is why 'we shipped everything we had' is a real
failure mode and not a joke.
what is in · what is deferred · and why this cut rather than another.
dependencies eliminate the impossible groupings, the ceiling caps the
size, the trade-offs choose among what is left.
the DONE condition is ASSEMBLED, never authored. you do not write a
wish list at the end — you walk what each rung already declared.
DONE = every item a conformance check against a DECLARATION
met the feature spec <- the contract
met the product spec <- the idea brief
goal of the function met <- the goal set here
looks EXACTLY like design <- design, approved before build
tests pass <- every proof layer declared by
documentation complete <- DERIVED, not declared: every
TWO ORPHANS RESOLVED WITHOUT NEW FUNCTIONS.
complete' had no upstream declaration when
this started. user testing turned out to be a
proof LAYER nobody had listed; documentation
turned out to be DERIVED rather than declared.
Does every DONE item point at a declaration that EXISTS?
if it does not, it cannot be checked — so it passes by ASSERTION.
that is the unqualified-risk failure in another costume: it looks
handled because it is written down.
fix it one of two ways: remove the item, or go and get the
declaration made upstream. never leave it unbacked.
MACHINE: every DONE item points at an existing declaration ·
the slice is within the comprehension ceiling.
HUMAN: Tony approves the grouping — what is in, what is deferred,
and why this cut rather than another.
→ Choose what matters next, then the loop
the DONE condition is what /loop terminates on. a loop with a vague
DONE condition is the one that runs forever — which is why the
assembly rule above is load-bearing rather than tidy.
